rv.q: Yet it offers a vivid, warming glimpse ofa comedy partnership made in and now consigned to Heaven.
But the show’s heart is in the right place and anyone who loves Eric and Ernie will find this affectionate tribute unexpectedly moving as well as funny.

It is, however, very funny and affecting and manifestly a labour of love by its deviser/performers, Jonty Stephens and Ian Ashpitel, who manage to recreate everything about their comic heroes with uncanny accuracy and finesse.

Trouble is, it's all gags, and nothing but gags, of the 'my father always got a bird for Christmas' variety. This is lapped up by card-carrying members of the Eric and Ernie fan club, but it does grow a bit wearisome.

Perhaps Eric and Ernie's was a rare comedy partnership built on harmony, not rivalry, but in the end it leaves the drama wanting. Instead, this is a chance to enjoy a masterful Morecambe and Wise tribute; it's a show that brings a bright ray of sunshine into the West End this winter.
It would be a hard heart that didn't warm to the sweet silliness of the evening.

The 90 minute two-hander has just about enough pizazz and exchange, and is not short of their brilliant gags including the stone-in-the-paper-bag routine, the ‘Grieg’s Piano Concerto’ sketch and the various digs at Des ‘Desperate’ O’Connor.
The show is touching as well as funny.

cn.t: Critics find this Morecambe & Wise tribute warmly nostalgic, with Stephens and Ashpitel's uncanny physical likenesses widely praised. Reception is broadly positive, though some note it plays better as fond remembrance than groundbreaking comedy.
